planting.note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; Ponca's upright, thornless canes need only a simple support and produce an unusually sweet, small-seeded berry prized for fresh eating.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the upright canes onto a simple two-wire trellis for support. Released by the University of Arkansas breeding program, Ponca is one of the newer thornless erect blackberry cultivars, notable for exceptionally high sugar content and small seed size that give it outstanding fresh-eating flavor compared to older, tarter cultivars. The compact, upright canes need less trellising than sprawling semi-erect types, and the plant produces a concentrated harvest over a relatively short picking window in early summer. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to make room for the canes that will fruit the following season.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

common_name: Prime-Ark Traveler Blackberry (Thornless Machine-Harvestable Primocane Blackberry)

planting.note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; as a primocane-fruiting type, Prime-Ark Traveler can produce a fall crop on new canes the same year it is planted, in addition to the following year's traditional summer crop.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and provide a sturdy trellis, since this vigorous primocane-fruiting cultivar produces fruit on first-year canes in addition to the traditional second-year floricane crop. Bred by the University of Arkansas specifically for firmness that withstands mechanical harvesting and shipping, Prime-Ark Traveler also performs well as a home-garden thornless blackberry, producing a first crop on primocanes in late summer and fall in addition to the normal early-summer floricane harvest. Because it fruits on both first- and second-year wood, pruning decisions affect which crop you prioritize: cutting all canes to the ground in winter sacrifices the floricane crop but still allows a fall primocane harvest, while leaving some canes standing provides both crops.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

common_name: Black Satin Blackberry (Classic Thornless Semi-Erect Blackberry)

planting.note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; Black Satin's sprawling canes need a sturdy trellis and regular tying through the season to keep the planting manageable.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the sprawling semi-erect canes onto a sturdy two-wire trellis. One of the earliest widely available thornless blackberry cultivars, introduced in the 1970s, Black Satin remains valued for its reliable, heavy production of large, glossy, firm black fruit with good flavor, ripening over a fairly long midsummer season. The semi-erect canes need more support and tying than fully upright modern cultivars, but the plant is vigorous, dependable, and tolerant of a range of soil conditions. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to keep the planting productive and make room for new fruiting canes.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

planting.note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; Chester ripens later in summer than most blackberry cultivars, extending the harvest season, and tolerates colder winters than many thornless types.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the vigorous semi-erect canes onto a sturdy trellis. Chester is one of the most widely planted thornless blackberry cultivars in North America, valued for a rare combination of good cold hardiness, strong resistance to cane blight and other diseases, and reliable production of large, firm, mild-flavored fruit that ripens later in summer than most cultivars, extending the blackberry harvest season. Its tolerance of colder winters than many thornless blackberries has made it a standard choice well beyond the Gulf South, though it performs well there too given adequate summer water. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to make room for the next season's fruiting canes.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

planting.note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; Rosborough was bred specifically for hot, humid Gulf South conditions and has thorns, unlike many modern thornless cultivars.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the semi-erect canes onto a sturdy trellis. Developed by the Texas A&M blackberry breeding program, Rosborough was selected specifically for reliable performance in the hot, humid conditions of Texas and the Gulf South, producing good yields of medium-to-large, flavorful berries in early-to-mid summer. It has thorns, unlike many newer cultivars, but its regional heat tolerance and disease resistance have made it a long-standing favorite among Gulf Coast growers who prioritize proven regional performance over the novelty of thornlessness. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to keep the planting vigorous and productive.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
